questions.stem: Which industry depends directly on the ethanol from fermentation?

options.explanation: Cheese relies on bacteria, not ethanol.
Refining is physical chemistry, not fermentation.
Bread needs the carbon dioxide, and ethanol evaporates away.
Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

questions.stem: Why can a sealed sugar solution still support yeast respiration?

options.text: Because yeast can respire without oxygen when glucose is available
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

questions.stem: State the word equation products when yeast ferments glucose.
questions.modelAnswer: Glucose is converted into ethanol and carbon dioxide during anaerobic respiration in yeast.

questions.stem: Name the process yeast cells use to respire without oxygen.
questions.modelAnswer: Yeast cells respire anaerobically, and the process is called fermentation.

questions.stem: Explain why fermentation is described as economically important.
questions.modelAnswer: Fermentation underpins two major industries at once, since carbon dioxide makes bread dough rise and ethanol forms the alcohol in drinks, so the same pathway earns money in bakeries and breweries.

questions.stem: A brewer finds her fermenting vat stopped bubbling. Suggest one cause tied to this pathway.
questions.modelAnswer: The glucose supply may be exhausted, because fermentation needs sugar to continue producing ethanol and carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: State why oil floats on the sugar solution in this practical.
questions.modelAnswer: The oil layer prevents oxygen from entering, so the yeast respires anaerobically.

questions.stem: Name the solution that tests for carbon dioxide in the second tube.
questions.modelAnswer: Limewater fills the second tube and turns cloudy when carbon dioxide bubbles through it.

questions.stem: Explain why the water bath temperature must be set and held steady.
questions.modelAnswer: Temperature changes enzyme activity, so a fixed bath temperature isolates it as the variable being tested while keeping every other condition constant.

questions.stem: A student's bubbles stop after five minutes at high temperature. Give the likely reason.
questions.modelAnswer: The enzymes in the yeast have denatured beyond their optimum, so fermentation halts and carbon dioxide production stops.

questions.stem: What pattern of bubble counts shows yeast respiration speeding up?

options.text: Counts stay flat at all temperatures
options.explanation: Temperature clearly changes the rate.
Cooling slows enzyme activity.

options.text: Counts rise as the water bath warms towards the enzymes' optimum
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Falling counts indicate denaturation setting in.

options.text: The yeast runs out of bubbles to recycle

Oil behaviour is not the cause.

options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

questions.stem: Which quantities belong in the controlled column of this investigation?

options.explanation: The organism is kept the same, a fixed choice.

options.text: Sugar concentration, solution volume, pH and the mass of yeast added
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Temperature is the changed variable.

questions.stem: A class repeats each temperature three times and averages the counts. Which evaluation letter does that strengthen?

options.explanation: The measure stayed bubbles per window.
Temperature is the intended independent variable.

options.text: R, because repeated readings make the results reliable
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
The organism stayed the same; repeats are reliability.

questions.stem: State what is measured and over what period in this practical.
questions.modelAnswer: The number of bubbles produced is counted in a fixed time period such as two minutes.

questions.stem: Name the variable that is changed between repeats in this investigation.
questions.modelAnswer: The temperature of the water bath is changed for each repeat of the practical.

questions.stem: Explain why the same species of yeast must be used at every temperature.
questions.modelAnswer: Different yeast strains carry different enzyme optima, so switching species would confound the temperature effect and break the fairness of the comparison.

questions.stem: A baker wants maximum dough rise without killing the yeast. Use the results pattern to advise.
questions.modelAnswer: Choose a warm setting near the yeast optimum, because bubble output peaks there, and avoid hotter settings where denaturation halts carbon dioxide production.
